mv_ask(): from a sentence to a tested R script

Source: vignettes/articles/mv-ask-guide.Rmd
mv-ask-guide.Rmd

Many people who need an IRT analysis know what they want to find out but not which functions, arguments and checks get them there. mv_ask() closes that gap. You describe the analysis in a sentence, and mirtverse writes the full, commented R script: reading the data, recoding missing values, fitting and checking the model, testing for DIF, scoring, plotting and reporting. You read the script, change it if you like, and then run or save it.

This article explains how mv_ask() works, walks through examples, and reports how accurately it understands requests with each of the supported language models.

library(mirtverse)
#> Loading required package: mirt
#> Loading required package: stats4
#> Loading required package: lattice

How it works

mv_ask() follows a hybrid design: a language model (or a built-in keyword parser) decides what to do, and mirtverse decides how to do it.

  1. Summarise the data. profile_data() describes each column: its type, number of distinct values, range, share missing and likely role (item, grouping variable, ID or response time). Individual responses are never part of this summary.
  2. Understand the request. The request and the summary go to the understanding step. By default this is a keyword parser that runs offline and needs no setup. If you connect a model with mv_ask_setup(), Claude, GPT or a local Ollama model does this step instead. The model never writes code. It fills in a structured form with a fixed set of choices: which columns are items, which model, how many dimensions, which grouping variable, which missing-value codes and which outputs.
  3. Check the plan. The filled-in form becomes an mv_plan() object, which is checked against your data before any code is written. Do the columns exist? Does the grouping variable have at least two groups? Is a 2PL being asked of items with more than two categories? Problems are reported in plain language, and anything mirtverse assumed is listed.
  4. Write the script. Tested templates turn the plan into R code that uses only mirt and mirtverse functions with checked arguments. The same templates power the code export in the workbench.
  5. Run or save. Nothing runs until you ask. run_script(scr, check = TRUE) first runs the whole script on simulated data shaped like yours, so any error shows up before your real data are touched.

Because the language model only chooses among options that mirtverse already knows how to code, a model cannot invent a function or an argument that does not exist. The worst a misunderstanding can do is produce a valid script for a different analysis than the one you meant, and the printed plan makes that easy to spot.

Examples

The examples use a small simulated data set: 800 students, twelve 0/1 items (Q1 to Q12), a gender column and a student ID. They use the built-in keyword parser (provider = "none") so that this page builds without an API key. With an AI model connected, the same requests work, and so does much freer wording.

set.seed(1)
a <- matrix(rlnorm(12, 0.2, 0.25))
d <- matrix(rnorm(12))
mydata <- data.frame(student_id = 1:800, simdata(a, d, 800, itemtype = "2PL"),
                     gender = rep(c("F", "M"), 400))
names(mydata)[2:13] <- paste0("Q", 1:12)

A complete analysis in one sentence 

scr <- mv_ask("Fit a 2PL, check DIF by gender and make a report",
              data = mydata, provider = "none")
scr
#> Request: Fit a 2PL, check DIF by gender and make a report 
#> Understood by the built-in keyword parser
#> 
#> Analysis plan
#>   - Data: mydata 
#>   - Items: 12 items (Q1 ... Q12) 
#>   - Model: 2PL, 1 dimension 
#>   - DIF by: gender 
#>   - Steps: fit, dif, report 
#> Assumptions
#>   - Used the 12 columns that look like item responses as items. 
#> 
#> R script (run it with run_script(), save it with save_script())
#> ----------------------------------------------------------------
#> # Analysis script written by mirtverse::mv_ask()
#> # 2026-10-30 19:17
#> # Request: Fit a 2PL, check DIF by gender and make a report
#> # Assumptions:
#> #  - Used the 12 columns that look like item responses as items.
#> library(mirtverse)
#> 
#> # Data
#> raw <- mydata
#> items <- raw[, c("Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4", "Q5", "Q6", "Q7", "Q8", "Q9", "Q10", "Q11",
#>   "Q12")]
#> group <- raw$gender
#> 
#> # Fit the 2PL model
#> mod <- mirt(items, 1, itemtype = "2PL")
#> glance(mod)
#> 
#> # Differential item functioning by gender
#> dif_res <- dif(items, group = group, model = "2PL")
#> dif_res
#> gg_dif(dif_res)
#> interpret(dif_res)
#> 
#> # Report
#> mv_report(mod, file = "mirtverse-report.html", dif = dif_res)

The printout has three parts: the plan (what will be done), the assumptions mirtverse made (here, that Q1 to Q12 are the items because they look like item responses), and the script itself.

Refining a script

Pass the script back with the change you want. The rest of the plan is kept.

scr <- mv_ask(scr, "use a 3PL instead and save EAP scores to scores.csv")
scr$plan
#> Analysis plan
#>   - Data: mydata 
#>   - Items: 12 items (Q1 ... Q12) 
#>   - Model: 3PL, 1 dimension 
#>   - DIF by: gender 
#>   - Steps: fit, dif, scores, report 
#> Assumptions
#>   - Used the 12 columns that look like item responses as items.

Letting mirtverse choose the model

When you don’t name a model, mirtverse compares the candidates with select_model() and keeps the best one.

mv_ask("Which IRT model fits my data best? Explain the results in plain language.",
       data = mydata, provider = "none")
#> Request: Which IRT model fits my data best? Explain the results in plain
#> language. 
#> Understood by the built-in keyword parser
#> 
#> Analysis plan
#>   - Data: mydata 
#>   - Items: 12 items (Q1 ... Q12) 
#>   - Model: compare candidate models and keep the best (1 dimension) 
#>   - Steps: fit, fitcheck, interpret 
#> Assumptions
#>   - Used the 12 columns that look like item responses as items. 
#> 
#> R script (run it with run_script(), save it with save_script())
#> ----------------------------------------------------------------
#> # Analysis script written by mirtverse::mv_ask()
#> # 2026-10-30 19:17
#> # Request: Which IRT model fits my data best? Explain the results in
#> #   plain language.
#> # Assumptions:
#> #  - Used the 12 columns that look like item responses as items.
#> library(mirtverse)
#> 
#> # Data
#> raw <- mydata
#> items <- raw[, c("Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4", "Q5", "Q6", "Q7", "Q8", "Q9", "Q10", "Q11",
#>   "Q12")]
#> 
#> # Choose and fit a model
#> sel <- select_model(items)
#> sel
#> mod <- sel$best
#> 
#> # Check model and item fit
#> item_table(mod)
#> gg_itemfit(mod)
#> gg_q3(mod)
#> 
#> # Plain-language summary
#> interpret(mod)

Missing-value codes and a subset of items 

coded <- mydata
coded$Q3[c(5, 17, 40)] <- 9
mv_ask("Rasch model for Q1 to Q10 only; 9 means missing. Give me person scores.",
       data = coded, provider = "none")$plan
#> Analysis plan
#>   - Data: coded 
#>   - Items: 10 items (Q1 ... Q10) 
#>   - Missing codes: 9 
#>   - Model: Rasch, 1 dimension 
#>   - Steps: fit, scores

Using an AI model

Connect a model once. The key is asked for in a masked prompt and stored in your .Renviron file or the system keychain, never in scripts or reports.

mv_ask_setup("claude")                         # Anthropic Claude, your own key
mv_ask_setup("openai")                         # OpenAI GPT, your own key
mv_ask_setup("ollama", model = "qwen3.8:27b")  # free, runs on your computer

After that, mv_ask() uses the model automatically, and requests can be as loose as you would write them to a colleague:

mv_ask("I want to know whether boys and girls with the same ability answer
        the items differently, and I need a report for my committee",
       data = mydata)

Claude and GPT usually answer within a few seconds. A model running locally through Ollama may take noticeably longer to return a plan, from several seconds to a minute or more, depending on the model’s size and your computer.

Seeing exactly what is sent

dry_run = TRUE prints what would be sent to the model without sending it. With anonymize = TRUE, column names are replaced by V1, V2, … (also inside your request) and category labels are dropped. mirtverse maps the names back on your computer.

mv_ask("check DIF by gender", data = mydata, anonymize = TRUE, dry_run = TRUE)
#> No AI model is set up, so nothing would be sent; an AI model would receive:
#> 
#> Request: check DIF by V14
#> 
#> Data: 800 rows, 14 columns.
#> Columns (name | type | distinct values | min | max | share missing | guessed role | categories):
#> - V1 | integer | 800 | 1 | 800 | 0.00 | id | 
#> - V2 | integer | 2 | 0 | 1 | 0.00 | item | 
#> - V3 | integer | 2 | 0 | 1 | 0.00 | item | 
#> - V4 | integer | 2 | 0 | 1 | 0.00 | item | 
#> - V5 | integer | 2 | 0 | 1 | 0.00 | item | 
#> - V6 | integer | 2 | 0 | 1 | 0.00 | item | 
#> - V7 | integer | 2 | 0 | 1 | 0.00 | item | 
#> - V8 | integer | 2 | 0 | 1 | 0.00 | item | 
#> - V9 | integer | 2 | 0 | 1 | 0.00 | item | 
#> - V10 | integer | 2 | 0 | 1 | 0.00 | item | 
#> - V11 | integer | 2 | 0 | 1 | 0.00 | item | 
#> - V12 | integer | 2 | 0 | 1 | 0.00 | item | 
#> - V13 | integer | 2 | 0 | 1 | 0.00 | item | 
#> - V14 | text | 2 |  |  | 0.00 | group |

Writing a plan by hand

The plan is an ordinary R object, so you can skip the request entirely:

pl <- mv_plan(items = "Q1:Q10", model = "Rasch",
              steps = c("describe", "fitcheck", "scores", "report"))
mv_ask(data = mydata, plan = pl)
#> Analysis plan
#>   - Data: mydata 
#>   - Items: 10 items (Q1 ... Q10) 
#>   - Model: Rasch, 1 dimension 
#>   - Steps: fit, describe, fitcheck, scores, report 
#> 
#> R script (run it with run_script(), save it with save_script())
#> ----------------------------------------------------------------
#> # Analysis script written by mirtverse::mv_ask()
#> # 2026-10-30 19:17
#> library(mirtverse)
#> 
#> # Data
#> raw <- mydata
#> items <- raw[, c("Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4", "Q5", "Q6", "Q7", "Q8", "Q9", "Q10")]
#> 
#> # Describe the items
#> itemstats(items)
#> 
#> # Fit the Rasch model
#> mod <- mirt(items, 1, itemtype = "Rasch")
#> glance(mod)
#> 
#> # Check model and item fit
#> item_table(mod)
#> gg_itemfit(mod)
#> gg_q3(mod)
#> 
#> # Person scores
#> scores <- augment(mod, method = "EAP")
#> gg_scores(mod)
#> 
#> # Report
#> mv_report(mod, file = "mirtverse-report.html")

How accurate is it?

We wrote 100 requests of the kind users actually type, from “1PL please” to “Fit a 2PL to my data, check DIF by gender, and make a report”, each with the plan a careful analyst would choose. A few are deliberately vague (such as “check DIF” when the data have several possible grouping columns), and the right response to these is to ask a question rather than guess. The requests and expected plans are in inst/benchmark/ask-requests.csv.

A plan counts as fully correct only if every field matches: whether a question was needed, the model, the number of dimensions, the grouping variable, the missing-value codes, the items and the analysis steps.

Percentage of the 100 benchmark requests understood correctly.
Parser Fully correct Question Model Dimensions Group Missing Items Steps
Claude (claude-opus-5-5) 95 96 99 100 99 100 100 98
OpenAI GPT (gpt-5.6-terra) 90 98 97 100 99 100 100 94
Ollama: Qwen 3.8 27B 84 94 98 100 100 99 100 92
Ollama: Qwen 3 8B 35 83 91 100 99 100 100 46
Built-in keyword parser* 98 100 100 100 100 100 100 98

* The keyword parser’s patterns were tuned on these same 100 requests, so its score is an upper bound. On new wording it will do worse, which is where the AI models earn their place.

What the results show:

  • Claude understood 95 of 100 requests completely, and no field fell below 96%. Its misses were mostly about whether to ask a clarifying question and which outputs to include.
  • GPT reached 90%. Its weakest field was the analysis steps (94%): it added or left out outputs, such as a report or plots, more often than Claude.
  • Local models (Ollama) keep everything on your computer and cost nothing per request, and model size matters a great deal. Qwen 3.8 27B reached 84%, not far behind GPT, with its misses spread over the steps (92%) and when to ask a question (94%). The smaller Qwen 3 8B got the model, items, group and missing codes right almost always, yet chose the right set of analysis steps only 46% of the time, so only 35% of its plans were fully correct. If you use a local model, pick the largest one your computer runs comfortably, and always read the printed plan before running the script.
  • Local models are slower. Claude and GPT usually return a plan within a few seconds. A model running through Ollama on your own computer can take much longer, from several seconds to a minute or more per request, depending on the model’s size and your hardware. Models that “think” before answering, such as the Qwen 3 family, are slower still.
  • Choosing the model, the items, the group and the missing codes is easy for every parser. The harder part is reading how much the user wants done (the steps) and noticing when a request is too vague to act on.

To run the benchmark yourself, for example to try another Ollama model:

mirtverse:::ask_benchmark("claude")
mirtverse:::ask_benchmark("openai")
mirtverse:::ask_benchmark("ollama", model = "qwen3.8:27b")

Each run sends the 100 requests with the column summary of a simulated data set. With Claude or GPT this costs roughly one or two US dollars. A local model costs nothing but takes much longer: on a recent Mac, Qwen 3.8 27B needed more than an hour for the 100 requests.

Privacy in brief

  • Individual responses are never sent. The model sees your request and the column summary from profile_data().
  • anonymize = TRUE hides column names and category labels.
  • dry_run = TRUE shows exactly what would be sent.
  • With Ollama, nothing leaves your computer at all.
  • Without any setup, the keyword parser runs fully offline.
